cards.front: Four systems that keep an agent healthy
cards.back: Traces (what happened in one run), metrics and alerts (is it healthy now), the audit log (provable record of who did what), and maintenance (drift checks and safe changes). They have different readers and rules.
Logs are for engineers: sampled, trimmed, editable, kept briefly. An audit log is evidence: complete, append-only, tamper-evident and kept for years. Keep them separate.

cards.front: Trace and span for an agent run
cards.back: A trace is the tree of steps for one run under one trace ID; each model call, tool call, retrieval and guardrail check is a span with timing and attributes such as model version and tokens.
Decide which traces to keep after the run ends: keep every failed, slow or down-voted trace and a few per cent of healthy ones.
Error budget = (1 − SLO) × runs in the window. Burn rate = observed error rate ÷ (1 − SLO); 1× spends the budget exactly over the window.
Page when the burn rate is about 14× over the last hour (2% of a 30-day budget gone in an hour); open a ticket when it stays above about 1× for days. Raw error-rate alerts page for blips.

cards.front: What makes an audit log acceptable to an auditor
cards.back: Tamper evidence: append-only entries, hash-chained, with the newest hash anchored outside the admins' reach (signed, WORM storage, trusted timestamp). Access controls alone can't prove nothing changed.
Each entry stores SHA-256 of the previous entry's hash plus its own content, so changing or deleting an old entry breaks every later hash.

cards.front: Why a hash chain needs an anchor
cards.back: An admin who controls the whole log can edit an entry and recompute every later hash. A head hash signed or stored outside their reach exposes the rebuilt chain.
Write once, read many: in compliance mode nobody, root included, can overwrite or delete objects until retention ends. A common home for audit logs and anchored checkpoints.

cards.front: Kinds of drift in a running agent
cards.back: Inputs (new topics), the model (provider updates behind an alias), tools and APIs, knowledge (stale documents), and cost and load. Pin versions and watch each on a dashboard.

cards.front: Incident levers to have before launch
cards.back: Rollback of prompt or model version, per-tool feature flags, a read-only mode, routing to humans, a fallback model and a kill switch for autonomous actions.

quiz.q: Your agent's audit logs live in a PostgreSQL table that administrators can update. An external auditor rejects them because nothing proves entries weren't altered. Which feature is most essential?
choices: Richer log entries that capture the full prompt and response
Stricter role-based access control and MFA for the administrators
Append-only, tamper-evident entries: each hashed and chained to the previous one, with checkpoints anchored or stored in WORM storage
Nightly backups of the table to a second database
quiz.why: Only tamper evidence lets an outsider verify that no entry changed; access controls and backups still rely on trusting the admins.

quiz.q: An attacker with full admin rights edits an old audit entry and recomputes every hash after it. What still exposes the change?
choices: The hash chain itself, because recomputed hashes are always invalid
The database's own row timestamps
A longer hash such as SHA-512
A head hash signed or stored outside the admins' reach no longer matches
quiz.why: A consistent rebuilt chain verifies on its own; only an external anchor reveals it.

quiz.q: With a 99.5% SLO, the error rate over the last hour is 7.2%. What should happen?
choices: Do nothing until the error budget is fully spent
Page on-call: the burn rate is about 14×, spending the month's budget in about two days
Lower the SLO to 92% so the alert stops
Open a low-priority ticket for next sprint

quiz.q: Answers got worse last Tuesday, with no deploy and no rise in errors. What is the most likely cause, and the prevention?
choices: Network latency; move to a closer region
Too few GPU replicas; add autoscaling
The provider updated the model behind an alias; pin exact model versions and run online evals
A memory leak in the API gateway; restart the pods nightly
quiz.why: Quality can drift with zero errors; pinned versions and online evals catch it.

quiz.q: You serve a 13B model in FP16 (about 26 GB per replica) on GPUs with FP8 support, and peak throughput is below target. You can't retrain. Which statement is correct?
choices: Quantization always requires retraining the model
Post-training 8-bit quantization roughly halves weight memory, freeing room for KV cache and larger batches, but accuracy must be validated
Quantization raises throughput with no accuracy impact at all
Quantizing the weights automatically shrinks the KV cache too
quiz.why: 8-bit PTQ needs no retraining and frees memory for batching, with a small accuracy risk to measure.

quiz.q: A 3B clinical-notes model takes 5 s per note in FP32 on an edge device, must return JSON in under 2 s, and the clinics have unreliable internet. What is the best approach?
choices: Use beam search so the JSON is more accurate
Switch to a 7B model for better accuracy
An optimised engine in FP16 with INT8 calibration, then accuracy validation on real notes
Send notes to a larger cloud model when the device is slow
quiz.why: Lower precision cuts memory and latency on the device; cloud fails offline and beam search is slower.

quiz.q: Customer email addresses start appearing in your tracing vendor's dashboards. What is the right fix?
choices: Turn tracing off for the agent
Ask the vendor to delete the data monthly
Sample fewer traces
Redact sensitive fields in the telemetry collector before export, and keep full payloads in an access-controlled store
quiz.why: Redact at the collector so data never leaves your network; keep traces for debugging.

quiz.q: During an incident the agent is issuing wrong refunds. What is the first move?
choices: Wait for the error budget alert to confirm
Mitigate: disable the refund tool with a feature flag or switch to read-only mode, then diagnose from traces
Retrain the model on the bad cases
Find the root cause in the traces before changing anything
quiz.why: Stop the harm first; diagnosis comes after mitigation.
